subjective.question: Write three characteristics of species. (1) Species is basic to classifying animals, and there is usually a clear and apparent difference between species. (2) Species differ in appearance, shape and form — e.g. the horse, donkey and zebra come from the same family (Equus) but are different species, with similarities in behavior and appearance yet clear differences. (3) Species do not interbreed in naturally occurring circumstances; cross mating is not biologically beneficial because the genes are not propagated further — e.g. the cross of a horse and an ass produces a mule, which is sterile.

In Israel, children have to live in a Kibbutz separate from their parents. Children in the Kibbutz coming from European descent had IQ scores above 100 points, whereas children from Oriental/African descent scored 80-90 points. After 4-5 years their scores were similar. Explain what you understand from this. This study shows the powerful effect of environment on measured intelligence. Initially the two groups differed markedly (above 100 vs 80-90 points), which could be taken as a hereditary/racial difference. However, when both groups were reared in the same Kibbutz environment — same upbringing, schooling, nutrition and stimulation, away from their different home environments — the gap disappeared within 4-5 years and the scores became similar. The conclusion is that the original difference was environmental, not genetic: given a common enriched environment, children of different descents achieve similar IQ levels. It also supports the handout's point that environmental influences can affect intelligence — the same individual tested again after several years in a changed environment can gain substantially (about 20 points).

Do environmental influences affect intelligence? Yes. Environmental influences can affect intelligence: if the same individual is tested again after a period of several years it is possible to gain about 20 points. Early stimulation is important, and children should be stimulated when younger. The Kibbutz evidence supports this: children of European descent scored above 100 and children of Oriental/African descent 80-90, but after 4-5 years of a shared environment their scores became similar. Twin data show both influences: monozygotic twins reared together correlate r = .92 on IQ, but reared separately the correlation falls to .88 (and school achievement to .66); in dizygotic twins and siblings it falls further, and in unrelated individuals to .25. So intelligence reflects an interaction of genes and experience.

Enlighten few concepts of Mendelian genetics. Mendelian genetics began with Mendel's studies on sweet peas planted outside the monastery walls: he noticed a certain pattern in the colors and then manipulated the plantation, from which the laws of inheritance were derived. Key concepts: (1) Inheritance is carried by discrete units (genes) located on chromosomes, received from both parents. (2) Genes occur in alternative forms; a trait may be dominant (expressed when present in a single copy) or recessive (expressed only when inherited from both parents, i.e. a double recessive). Many behavioral and biochemical disorders follow this pattern — e.g. phenylketonuria results from a double recessive gene, and schizophrenia may arise from a recessive gene from both parents or a dominant gene from one parent. (3) Offspring therefore show predictable patterns of resemblance and difference. Mendel's work went unnoticed for fifty years but came into eminence in the 1900s, and it laid the basis of behavioral genetics — the study of how much genes contribute towards behavior.

How does evolution affect genes? Evolution acts on the gene pool of a species over generations. Environmental pressures — migration, environmental variation and the struggle for existence (concepts introduced by Buffon and used by Darwin) — bring about small heritable changes: traits that help survival and reproduction are propagated, while unfit combinations disappear. Lamarck proposed transmutation and use and disuse (organs grow and shrink from use, with change directed towards higher forms), while the modern view is that change, not fixity of species, is the rule (against Linnaeus, who believed species were fixed and unchanging). Within the gene pool, repeated use of the same pool (inbreeding) leads to expression of recessive genes, whereas cross-breeding between species does not propagate genes further (e.g. the sterile mule). Thus evolution continuously reshapes which genes survive in a population.

What do the twin studies narrate about schizophrenia? Twin studies show schizophrenia is a genetically inherited disorder. The incidence of schizophrenia in the general population is 1%. This rises if there is a close relative with schizophrenia: with siblings and dizygotic twins it rises to 10-15%, and the expectancy if one parent has it is about the same (10-15%). If both parents have it, the expectancy rises to 40-65%. A review of 17 studies (1928-1972) from all over the world showed the highest incidence among monozygotic (MZ) twins and lower among DZ twins. Rosenthal's (1959) study on MZ twins with schizophrenia reported 60% concordance; Inouye (1961) in Japan found 74% concordance for chronic schizophrenia in MZ twins. Schizophrenia is attributed to chemical, neural and biological imbalances created by genetic codes — possibly a recessive gene from both parents or a dominant gene from one parent.

What do studies show about schizophrenia in foster children? The classic study by Heston (1966) followed 50 children born to schizophrenic mothers and separated from them within a few days after birth, with 50 children born to normal mothers as controls. There was a much higher incidence of schizophrenia, personality disorder and other abnormalities in the children of schizophrenic mothers (47/50): 5 were schizophrenic, 4 mentally retarded, 9 antisocial and 13 had neurotic personalities. In the controls there were only 2 with personality disorders and 7 with neurotic personalities. Since the children were reared away from their schizophrenic mothers, the outcome cannot be explained by the home environment; there is strong evidence linking schizophrenia with genes transmitted to the offspring.

Are the humans born with fixed action patterns? Yes. A fixed action pattern is a preprogrammed sequence of behavior that is set in motion by a cue (sign stimulus) and carried through to completion. Sign stimuli lead to fixed action patterns in one animal, which then lead to a response in another. In humans too, fixed action patterns exist: for example, the infant turns away from noxious stimuli and smiles at pleasant ones. The neonate's reflexes — rooting, suckling, Moro, grasping, plantar — are further examples of inborn, preprogrammed patterns present at birth.

Define anterograde tracer and retrograde tracer. Tracers are substances injected into the nucleus of a neuron or other areas such as the synapse, and then followed through, in order to identify the structure, form and connections of cells. An anterograde tracer is one whose direction of transport is toward the periphery: the tracer is carried away from the cell soma to the projections (dendrites and their branches). A retrograde tracer is one whose direction of transport is towards the cell: the tracers move towards the cell soma, entering from the synapse; this shows the connections and interactions of a neuron. Major tracing techniques include radio labeling, autoradiography and horseradish peroxidase (HRP).

Explain any two neuropsychological measures. (1) WAIS as a neuropsychological test: the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) and Wechsler Children's Intelligence Scale (WISC) are used as part of the Halstead Reitan Battery. If a patient scores low on the verbal as compared to the performance tests, a left hemisphere deficit can be suspected; poor Picture Completion suggests memory and visual-spatial deficits (right hemisphere functions); poor Block Design indicates left/right posterior parietal damage. (2) Tests of language and lateral dominance: the Sodium Amytal test, in which an anesthetic is injected into the carotid artery so that one side of the brain is anaesthetized and cannot function or respond; and the dichotic listening test, in which words or sounds are given simultaneously to both ears and the preferred ear responds. In addition, the Harris Tests of Lateral Dominance are 11 quick tests assessing dominance of eye, ear, foot and hand. Neuropsychological assessment is used to localize damage, to assess cognitive functions (memory, language, intelligence, attention, perceptual and motor functions) and to evaluate whether treatment or therapy has been effective.

WAIS is an intelligence test. How is it/can it be used as a neuropsychological test? The general intelligence tests — Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) and Wechsler Children's Intelligence Scale (WISC) — are used as part of the Halstead Reitan Battery. Their subtest pattern, rather than the total IQ alone, localizes brain dysfunction: if a patient scores low on the verbal tests as compared to the performance tests, we can suspect a left hemisphere deficit; if Picture Completion performance is poor, we suspect memory and visual-spatial deficits, which are right hemisphere functions; poor performance on Block Design indicates left/right posterior parietal damage. Thus a general intelligence test becomes a neuropsychological instrument for assessing hemispheric functioning and the site of damage.

What do you know about MRI? MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) is a brain-scanning technique used to study the structure of the living brain without surgery. Its functional form, functional MRI (fMRI), is used when we want to test how different brain parts are used during an activity such as learning: the subject is asked to remember a list of words while the brain is functioning, and the images obtained are a clear indication of the areas where most activity is taking place or most oxygen is being used. MRI thus belongs to the research methods and techniques for the assessment of brain function, alongside CT (computed axial tomography) and PET, in which 2-DG glucose is injected into the carotid artery for brain scanning.

Explain any two of the following: Electroencephalography (EEG), EOG, EMG, Polygraphic recording. (1) Electroencephalography (EEG): the electrical activity of the brain is recorded from electrodes placed on the scalp; it shows the brain's ongoing activity and its changes during states such as sleep, waking and stimulation. (2) Polygraphic recording: simultaneous recording of several physiological measures at the same time — e.g. EEG (brain), EOG (electro-oculograph: eye movements) and EMG (electromyograph: muscle activity/tension) — so that a complete picture of the organism's state (as in sleep research) is obtained. EOG records eye movements through electrodes placed near the eyes, and EMG records muscle activity through electrodes placed over muscles; together these measures are the standard polygraphic set used in behavioral neuroscience research.

Explain Von Baer's (Van Baer's) animal study. Van Baer (1792-1876), a pre-Darwinian evolutionary theorist, studied the embryos of various animals and provided evidence against preformation (Aristotle's idea that the zygote is a mini individual preformed into the shape it will be born in). Since he saw similarities in the various animal embryos he studied, he stated that the young stages of higher animals resemble the young stages of lower animals — all embryos have the same shape and form — and that all animals higher on the evolutionary scale go through the various developmental stages of animals lower on the scale. He was correct in assuming there are no pre-formations: general features of all animal embryos appear earlier than special features (e.g. embryonic gill pouches in mammals as well as fishes, and similar brain development until specialized development takes place). His premises logically led to Haeckel's concept that ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny.

Mention some of the reflexes of a neonate. The reflexes of the neonate show a well documented development and progression of brain and body: Plantar reflex — if the foot of the neonate is stroked, the toes fan up and out. Rooting — if a cheek is softly touched, the newborn turns the mouth towards the touched cheek. Suckling — if an object is placed in the mouth, the newborn starts sucking; this is readiness for feeding. Moro response — if there is a sudden noise, the newborn stretches out at first and then hugs itself together. Grasping — if a round object or finger is placed against the fingers, the fingers curl around it, forming a very strong grip. Other reflexes include swimming, vomiting, hiccough, sneezing, yawning and blinking (normally within an hour after birth).

Being a student of "neurological bases of behavior", it is important to be aware of brain development before birth. Explain how the process begins and how it undergoes. Brain development before birth proceeds through embryogenesis and histogenesis. Embryogenesis — the process of development during the embryonic stages — includes induction, neurulation, vesicle formation and neural proliferation. In neurulation the neural tube is formed by rapid cell multiplication and division; on the 21st day the tube fuses, and groups of cells break away to form somites and the neural crest, which develop into the peripheral nervous system and ganglia; the inside of the tube (neural canal) remains as the ventricular zone where further development takes place. Differentiation and induction are the key changes: the three germ layers are initially totipotential (stem cells), and a trigger restricts the direction of growth so specialization begins. Histogenesis follows — neurons specialize and move to relevant neuroanatomical sites through cellular differentiation, determination, cellular maturation, cell migration, cell aggregation, cell competition and cell death. Growth (axonal growth and synapse formation) comes last. Throughout, there is a complex interaction of genes and environment: genes predetermine layers, shape and form, while the environment provides the trigger for the genetic program. The brain and body grow following the cephalo-caudal (head-to-tail) principle.

Cell migration is an inside-out process. The growing cells form three layers: internal, middle, and cell free zone. Briefly introduce these three layers. Cell migration is an inside-out process: cells move from the inside of the neural tube towards the outside. The growing cells form three layers. (1) The Internal layer: the innermost layer, which has cells that are still dividing. (2) The Middle layer: consists of cell bodies which eventually form grey matter; these cells do not divide after this, and these are the same cells found in the adult brain. (3) The Cell free zone: contains the fibre processes of the first two layers and is as yet empty of cells; migration is still taking place. Once cells reach their destination they grow dendrites and axons, sprouting growth cones, to develop synapses.

What do you know about the chemoaffinity hypothesis? The chemoaffinity hypothesis states that the undeveloped nervous system has a blueprint in the form of specific chemical, biological/mechanical pathways which the growing axons would follow to get to their destination. In other words, each growing axon is guided by chemical signals/markers to its specific target, so that the precise wiring of the nervous system is chemically specified. It is one of the hypotheses explaining how, during development, axons find their correct destinations among a huge number of cells (related ideas include the topographic gradient hypothesis and synaptic rearrangement).

How does the process of development and differentiation stop, and who controls this process? Development is self-regulating — it is a process regulated by itself. Cells proliferate at more than 40 times the normal adult level (neurons are formed at about 20,000 per minute, and about 1.5 times more cells than the adult brain are produced); the excess is then removed by cell death, which follows set principles. The full regulatory sequence is: cell proliferation (cells dividing and increasing in number), cell migration (cells travelling from inside toward the outside to their destinations), maturation (developing extensions), interconnections formed (connections with other cells), and cell death (cells die off). Evidence of self-regulation: muscles move without sensory input or stimulation, and nuclei develop even if isolated from the organs or denervated. A small piece of ectodermal tissue removed early is replaced by proliferation of neighbouring cells, whereas the same surgery done later leaves a permanent deficit — showing the process is internally programmed and time-bound. The growth spurt (10th-18th week of gestation) is the period of maximal cell formation and organization, when the embryo is most sensitive to radiation, chromosomal anomalies and viral infections.

Differentiate between differentiation and induction. Induction is the process during embryogenesis in which one tissue triggers the development/differentiation of another — the trigger by which the genetic program is set in motion. The three germ cell layers are initially all exactly the same (totipotential — stem cells); if the trigger for change does not occur, the layers would simply keep growing in size without becoming brain or other organs. Differentiation is the resulting process of specialization: cells become restricted in their direction of growth and take on specific forms and functions (as part of histogenesis, neurons differentiate, are determined, mature, migrate, aggregate, compete and die). Genes predetermine the layers and the shape and form they eventually take, while the environment provides the trigger (induction) for the genetic program to take place.

Differentiate between the molar and molecular perspectives in behavioral neuroscience. The level of analysis within the brain varies from studying the behavior of a large number of neurons to studying just one under the microscope. The molar view focuses on groups of networks, neurons or neuroanatomical areas — the larger units and their combined functioning. The molecular investigation focuses on single units, single cell, single molecule, single impulse and the brain-behavior relationships at that micro level. Behavioral neuroscience studies the brain-behavior relationship across this whole range, from molar to molecular — a universe within the small cranium of millions of neurons and glial cells.

Explain two ways of brain-behavior interaction. Brain and behavior influence each other in both directions. (1) Brain to behavior: the structure and activity of the brain produce and control behavior — e.g. degeneration of the basal ganglia produces Huntington's chorea; lesions of the hippocampus severely affect memory formation; stimulation of the amygdala produces a rage reaction; and neurotransmitter systems (neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, neuroregulators, neurohormones) regulate ongoing behavior, motivation and hormonal states. (2) Behavior/experience to brain: experience and behavior in turn change the brain — learning requires cells to change shape and form (microfilaments and microtubules are continuously formed and broken down as the cell changes); environmental stimulation in early life changes IQ performance (Kibbutz study), and during development the environment provides the triggers for genetic programs. Thus the brain-behavior relationship is bidirectional.

Name any three chromosomal abnormalities and briefly describe one. Three chromosomal abnormalities discussed in this course are: (1) Lesch-Nyhan syndrome — due to a recessive gene carried on the X chromosome, found only in males; symptoms are cerebral palsy, involuntary movements of the limbs, hands, feet and facial muscles, and self-mutilation of lips, mouth and fingers. (2) Klinefelter's syndrome — an extra X chromosome (XXY) in males. (3) Turner's syndrome — a single X chromosome (XO) in females. (XYY syndrome is another example.)
